concepts.title: Anti-causal Filters
concepts.one_liner: An anti-causal filter is a filter where the output depends only on future values, such that $h [n,m,t ]=0$ for all $t>0$.
concepts.content: Anti-causal filters are defined as the opposite of causal filters; in these systems, the output depends only on the future. Formally, a filter is anti-causal if $h [n,m,t ]=0$ for all $t>0$.
concepts.motivation_md: Anti-causal filters are used in theoretical signal processing and non-real-time applications where future data points are available, allowing for processing that considers subsequent inputs.
concepts.recap_md: - An anti-causal filter's output depends exclusively on future inputs.

key_passage.text: This is the opposite, when the output only depends on the future: $h \left[n,m,t \right]=0$ for all $t>0$.

concepts.title: Heaviside Step Function
concepts.one_liner: The Heaviside step function $u[t]$ is an infinite length function that is 0 for $t < 0$ and 1 otherwise.
concepts.content:
The Heaviside step function, $u [t]$, is an infinite length function defined as:
$$
u [t] = \begin{cases}
    0     & \quad \text{if }  t <0 \\
    1     & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$

[FIGURE:3bdfa12be361a5d6 | ]
concepts.motivation_md: The Heaviside step function is a fundamental tool in signal processing used to represent signals that switch on at a specific time and stay on indefinitely.

concepts.title: Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) Filters
concepts.one_liner: Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters are filters described by difference equations where the impulse response has infinite support.
concepts.content: Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support. They are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters. IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are those that, given a bounded input $| \ell _{in} [n,m,t ] |<A$, produce a bounded output $| \ell _{out} [n,m,t ] | <B$. For stability to occur, the impulse response must be bounded. In unstable filters, the amplitude of the impulse response diverges to infinity. For example, a filter may be stable if and only if $| \alpha | < 1$.
concepts.motivation_md: IIR filters are used to model systems where the current output depends on all previous inputs, allowing for efficient recursive implementations of complex frequency responses.
concepts.recap_md: - IIR filters have an impulse response that never returns to zero indefinitely.

concepts.title: Nulling Filter
concepts.one_liner: A nulling filter is a filter designed to cancel objects moving at a specific velocity by computing derivatives along space-time orientations.
concepts.content: A nulling filter $h$ is designed to cancel any objects moving at a specific velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. By using different filters, each one computing derivatives along different space-time orientations, output sequences can be created where specific objects disappear, as shown in @fig-tunedfilter.
concepts.motivation_md: Nulling filters are essential in computer vision and motion analysis to isolate or remove specific moving components from a video sequence based on their velocity.
concepts.recap_md: - A nulling filter removes objects moving at a specific velocity from a sequence.

concepts.title: Constant Brightness Assumption
concepts.one_liner: The constant brightness assumption posits that the brightness of pixels remains unchanged as a scene moves.
concepts.content: The constant brightness assumption is the premise that the brightness of pixels does not change while the scene is moving. This assumption allows for the use of continuous values for $x$, $y$, and $t$ in image functions $\ell_0(x,y)$, facilitating the calculation of various velocity values in motion analysis.
concepts.motivation_md: This assumption is a cornerstone of optical flow and motion estimation algorithms, providing a necessary constraint to solve for pixel movement between consecutive frames.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes pixel intensity is invariant under motion over short time intervals.

key_passage.text: This function also assumes that the brightness of the pixels does not change while the scene is moving (constant brightness assumption).

motivation.text: We use continuous values for x, y, and t, and continuous images, ℓ₀(x,y), because it allows us to deal with any velocity values.

concepts.title: Sinc Function

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

concepts.one_liner: The sinc function is the Fourier Transform of a box kernel, characterized by decreasing oscillations.
concepts.content:
The sinc function is the Fourier Transform (FT) of a box kernel. In the continuous domain, the sinc function is defined as:
$$
\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}
$$
This function reaches its maximum at $x=0$ and exhibits decreasing oscillations as $x$ moves away from the origin.

[FIGURE:cddd5de71ef162b7]
concepts.motivation_md: The sinc function is fundamental in signal processing and sampling theory, as it represents the ideal 'low-pass filter' in the frequency domain.

key_passage.text: The sinc function is the FT of a box kernel. In the continuous domain, the sinc function has the form: sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). This function has its maximum at x=0 and then has decreasing oscillations.

concepts.title: Causal Filters
concepts.one_liner: Causal filters are systems where the output depends only on current and past input values.
concepts.content: Causal filters are filters with output variations that only depend on the past values of the input. This requirement imposes the constraint that the impulse response $h[n,m,t] = 0$ for all $t < 0$. Consequently, if the input is an impulse at $t=0$, the output will only have non-zero values for $t > 0$. Under this condition, the filter output depends solely on the input's past for any possible input signal.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-time systems, we cannot use information from the 'future.' Causal filters are the only types of filters that can be implemented in real-time physical systems.
concepts.recap_md: - Output depends only on past and present inputs, not future ones.

key_passage.text: These are filters with output variations that only depend on the past values of the input. This puts the following constraint: $h \left[n,m,t \right]=0$ for all $t<0$.

motivation.text: If this condition is satisfied, then the filter output will only depend on the input's past for all possible inputs.

concepts.title: Non-causal Filters
concepts.one_liner: Non-causal filters are systems where the output depends on future input values.
concepts.content: Non-causal filters are filters where the output has a dependency on future inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: While physically impossible in real-time, non-causal filters are useful in post-processing applications (like image editing or recorded audio) where the entire signal is already available.
concepts.recap_md: - Output depends on future input values.

key_passage.text: When the output has a dependency on future inputs.
